channel.title: Kristopher Baker
channel.description: Product engineer with deep iOS roots, building user-facing features and the systems and tools behind them. Based in Tokyo.

item.title: KiFinder's source is public
item.content:encoded:
I have published the KiFinder source on GitHub under GPLv3, following the source-only decision from July.

I still do not offer a prebuilt app. To try it, you build it yourself with Xcode 26 and XcodeGen on an Apple silicon Mac. The face-model weights require a separate one-time download, and everything after that runs on the Mac. The README covers setup, the model, and how to sign it with your own team.

item.title: Fixing settings titles at the largest text size
item.content:encoded:
Sarukani's screenshot tour found four settings titles truncated at the largest Dynamic Type size. The rows measured the explanatory text correctly, but the title labels could give their parent a one-line ideal height. When the layout came back at that height, longer titles ended in an ellipsis.

The shared SettingLabel now fixes its vertical size while still allowing horizontal wrapping. Three standalone rows use the same rule. I added hosted layout tests for the settings page because they render real SwiftUI views in a window and catch the sizing behavior without paying for a full UI launch on every case.

This matches the verification split I use in the project. The package suite has 647 tests and runs in about 1.7 seconds. The app unit bundle has 200 tests and takes about 56 seconds because it includes rendered layout cases. The 17 UI tests take about 222 seconds, while the light-and-dark capture tour takes at least four minutes. Captures remain useful, but once one exposes a layout rule, a hosted test provides the cheaper regression check.

item.title: Why KiFinder will be source-only
item.content:encoded:
I have decided not to release KiFinder as a signed app, whether free or paid. Privacy drives that decision. The preschool albums I use it with contain hundreds of photos of children from many families. I can judge for myself whether to run face matching locally on my Mac to find my own daughter. Packaging the same capability for any album would require a different decision, and I do not feel comfortable making it.

The ArcFace model also sets a condition for any broader release. Its weights were trained on MS-Celeb-1M, which was withdrawn because it was built from people's faces without their consent. I can use that model for a personal tool, but I do not want to distribute it. An app release would first require finding or training a model on consented data. It would also mean taking on the review and support work for a Mac app.

I still want other engineers to inspect the approach. I plan to publish the source under GPLv3 instead of distributing an app. People can read it or build it for themselves, while derivative work will have to remain open.

item.title: Fixing the sandboxed Core ML path
item.content:encoded:
After I enabled the App Sandbox, KiFinder scans completed with zero detected faces. The progress UI still finished, which made the failure look like a valid album with no matches.

The Core ML setup compiled its model into a hard-coded directory under /private/tmp. A sandboxed app could not write there, the session failed to initialize, and a try? converted that error into nil for every embedding. I fixed it by deriving the scratch directory from the system temporary directory, which places it inside the app container.

I checked the change with the real engine over saved photos. The broken build produced zero embeddings; the fixed build produced five and six for the same inputs. I also stopped re-scoring the full album after every keep or skip. Re-scoring now runs from an explicit “Find new matches” action and uses one batched matrix multiplication per album.

The missing error handling still needs improvement. A model that cannot initialize should stop the scan and explain the failure instead of returning an empty result that looks successful.

item.title: Separating generated and author-provided furigana
item.content:encoded:
Aoede's furigana errors came from two different sources, so I built a small harness to separate them before changing the reader. FuriganaQA runs the production pipeline over Aozora books and compares each result with the ruby supplied in the text. Each mismatch comes from something the generator should have produced or a reading it could not infer.

The first group exposed fixable problems. Aoede took phonetic forms from OpenJTalk, causing long vowels to use phonetic spellings instead of the expected spelling. It also grouped mixed kanji runs too broadly. Switching to orthographic readings and using JmdictFurigana for per-kanji placement fixed those cases, with JMdict validating the result.

The second group includes readings chosen by an author, such as 本気 read as マジ. No analyzer can recover that choice from the characters. Aoede now preserves ruby from Aozora markup and EPUB <ruby> elements, gives it priority over generated furigana, and uses it for speech as well as display.

The harness made the boundary testable: published ruby wins when it exists, dictionaries handle known readings, and OpenJTalk fills the remaining gaps.

item.title: Adding the KiFinder review app
item.content:encoded:
KiFinder now has a Mac app around the matching engine. I can enroll a person by dropping in five to twelve reference photos, choose an album or the preschool's zip files, and review the scan without typing photo identifiers into a command.

The app splits the review into three groups. Confident matches start selected, borderline scores appear under “Worth a look,” and the remaining photos stay out of the main path. I can change every decision before saving. In a group photo, the inspector draws a box around each detected face and lets me choose the intended person. That avoids treating the highest-scoring face as the answer when several people are in the photo.

The kept photos go into a library grouped by person and month, ready to export to Photos. The app still writes the same manifest as the command-line engine, so the UI did not need a second data format. The UI presents decisions the engine already records.

For the screenshots I enrolled myself and used synthetic faces for everyone else. That kept the demo useful without putting a preschool album on a public page.

item.title: Switching Kokoro from Core ML to MLX
item.content:encoded:
Aoede's first Kokoro integration ran through FluidAudio and Core ML. They offered the natural on-device path, but the integration crashed on my M5 Mac with every compute option I tried. The GPU reported a Metal JIT error, while CPU and the Neural Engine failed lower in BNNS. The same library worked on older Apple silicon, so the model itself probably did not cause the problem.

I replaced that runtime with an MLX port of Kokoro. MLX runs on the M5 and provides a timestamp for each token, which improved the synchronized word highlight at the same time. It does require the Metal toolchain and a real GPU, so the provider belongs in the app target rather than a package built with plain swift build. The iOS Simulator cannot run it and falls back to Apple speech.

I kept the Core ML work on a branch in case its hardware support changes. For now, MLX fits better because it works on the machines I use and gives the reader more precise timing.

item.title: JPResume: Turning a Western Resume Into a Japanese One
item.content:encoded:
In the last couple of months, two different people asked if I could share my Japanese-style resume rather than my English one. They wanted the 履歴書 and 職務経歴書, the formats Japanese companies actually ask for when you apply.

Both times, I gave the same awkward answer: “let me get back to you on that.”

My English resume looked decent. I had only a pile of half-finished notes for the Japanese one, already out of date the moment I touched the English version. I would not rewrite both by hand every job cycle in a second language.

So I built JPResume, a small Swift CLI that turns a western-style resume into both Japanese formats and keeps them in sync.

Why a Japanese Resume Requires Different Work

If you have only written western resumes, you might treat the Japanese versions as a translation job. Translation alone does not solve the problem.

A 履歴書 (rirekisho) uses a grid form: name, furigana, photo slot, education and work history with year/month columns, licenses, 志望動機, and 本人希望記入欄. Conventions govern how to mark your current role, end the work history section with 「現在に至る」, and choose western years or Japanese era dates. Some companies care about these details. Some do not. Nothing makes them obvious the first time.

A 職務経歴書 (shokumukeirekisho) provides the free-form counterpart. The actual career story lives here: 職務要約, role details, skills, achievements, and 自己PR. Writing in those phrasing conventions takes its own skill. “Helped increase sign-ups by about 30%” reads naturally in English. In Japanese, something like 新規会員登録数の約30%増加に寄与 fits better.

The two formats also create an alignment problem. Your English and Japanese resumes need to tell the same story, with the same dates, titles, and emphasis. When they drift, you usually notice at the worst possible moment.

A tool can help keep those versions aligned.

How It Works

I kept the pipeline boring on purpose: deterministic where possible, LLM-assisted where useful, and reviewable in between.

flowchart LR
    parse[Parse]
    normalize["Normalize (LLM)"]
    repair[Repair]
    validate[Validate]
    generate["Generate (LLM)"]
    render[Render]

    parse --> normalize --> repair --> validate --> generate --> render

Parse stays deterministic. It accepts markdown, DOCX, or PDF and produces a rough structured version. Markdown goes through a parser. DOCX and PDF go through text preprocessing, because once text comes out of those formats, most of the structure disappears. Scanned PDFs fall back to Vision OCR.

The LLM first appears during Normalize. It combines the parsed resume with the Japan-specific facts in jpresume_config.yaml, including the kanji name, furigana, address, education, and certifications, then produces a normalized structure. Dates become real integers. The stage classifies bullets as achievements or responsibilities and groups skills into categories. The prompt explicitly tells the model not to invent anything and asks it to flag ambiguous dates with low confidence rather than guess.

Repair returns to deterministic processing. It sorts roles, reconciles overlapping dates, and fixes is_current inconsistencies. Validate surfaces what remains: overlaps, low-confidence entries, suspicious gaps, or total years that look off.

Generate produces the rirekisho and shokumukeirekisho JSON. Render turns those into markdown and native PDFs using CoreGraphics and Hiragino Sans, so the Japanese typography looks intentional instead of falling back to an awkward default.

If you have built AI-assisted tooling, this pipeline will look familiar: keep control where you can, use the model where it helps, and put a human-readable artifact between stages.

The Workflow I Actually Use

The CLI can run end to end:

jpresume convert resume.md --provider claude-cli --format both

That works. But for most changes, I use the agent skill because it supports the workflow I wanted: external mode.

In external mode, the LLM stages do not call a provider directly. They write a prompt bundle to disk and exit. An agent such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex reads the bundle, produces the response JSON, writes it back, and re-runs the stage with --ingest.

In other words, the agent supplies the model output.

That sounds like an implementation detail, but it changes the experience. The agent sees every prompt and every response. It can pause, ask me a question, fix a bad field, and re-ingest without restarting the whole pipeline. When it normalizes a role, I can see exactly how it interpreted the dates before anything downstream depends on them. If something looks wrong, I can edit the JSON instead of running a full re-prompt.

I probably would have gotten this wrong in a one-shot tool. One-shot generation works for a first draft. For a document I might send to a company, I need the review loop.

The Honest Limits

So far, I have tested JPResume on only one resume: mine.

That resume has a specific shape. One country of origin. A software engineering career. Company names that Japanese recruiters likely recognize. Relatively clean dates. A JLPT certification that maps neatly to standard phrasing. It does not cover every edge case: career switches, international graduate programs, long intentional gaps, unusual role titles, or industries where Japanese resume conventions differ from tech.

I would not be surprised if the first outside resume exposes something the normalizer handles poorly, or a phrasing pattern the generator does not produce gracefully. I designed the pipeline to make those fixes cheap: edit an artifact and re-run one stage. I have not seen those cases yet. My sample size is one.

So if you try it and something looks wrong, or you know a resume shape it should handle better, I would like to hear about it. I welcome issues, pull requests, or notes. The README contains the install instructions and agent skill.

What I Would Keep Even If the Tool Changes

I expect the pipeline shape to outlast this implementation: deterministic parsing, strict no-invention normalization, a deliberate validation pause, and external mode so an agent can act as the model while still reviewing its own output.

That pattern works beyond Japanese resumes. It fits any document where a fabricated field costs too much and a fully automated one-shot does not fit: regulatory filings, contracts, internal reports, anything with structure and consequences.

For now, JPResume turns a markdown resume into a 履歴書 and 職務経歴書 that I would actually hand to a company.

Now I have one source to update before the next time someone asks me for both documents.

item.title: Remote Dev Setup With Real Constraints
item.content:encoded:
I wanted to pull out my phone on a train in Japan, reconnect to a dev session running on my Mac at home, and keep working. That does not seem like such a strange thing to want anymore. But getting it to work reliably from a phone without blowing up my existing setup took more work than I expected.

And then, right around the time I got it working, Claude Code shipped Remote Control and Dispatch. More on that later.

Why I Didn't Just Use Tailscale

If someone told me they wanted private remote access to their personal machine, I would probably tell them to use Tailscale and move on with their life. It is a great tool. For plenty of people it solves the whole problem.

But my situation was a little stranger than that. My Mac runs a work VPN, and I did not want to mix personal and company Tailscale accounts on the same machine. I did not want to expose my home network to inbound connections from the public internet. And because I planned to use this from my phone, often on mobile data between Wi-Fi networks, I needed the connection to survive the kind of interruptions that kill a normal SSH session.

I could easily work around any one of those constraints alone. Together, they ruled out the cleaner-looking options. The remaining setup looks less elegant on a diagram, but it fits those constraints.

The Shape of the Thing

The final setup forms a chain, and each link exists for a specific reason:

flowchart LR
    phone[Phone]
    mosh[mosh]
    vps[VPS]
    reverse[reverse SSH]
    mac[Mac]
    tmux[tmux]
    tools[Claude Code]

    phone --> mosh --> vps --> reverse --> mac --> tmux --> tools

My phone connects to a small VPS using mosh, which covers the part of mobile networking that plain SSH struggles with: changing IPs, switching between Wi-Fi and cellular, and recovering from drops without leaving you staring at a frozen cursor. Only the VPS has a public address. My Mac reaches it through an outbound reverse SSH tunnel, which means the Mac never needs to accept inbound traffic from the internet at all. And tmux on the Mac turns the whole thing from a fragile connection into a persistent session I can detach from and come back to later.

That last part surprised me. Once the session itself became durable, I could return to work already in progress instead of reconnecting from scratch.

Where It Actually Broke

Most of what I learned came from the failures, not the original plan.

The reverse tunnel could go half-dead after sitting idle. Port 22 continued listening on the VPS. The connection looked fine. But the session behind it had gone stale, so jumping to the Mac would just hang. Fixing it meant treating liveness as a real concern on both sides: SSH keepalives from the Mac, autossh to rebuild the tunnel when it dropped, and a VPS-side script that checked whether localhost:22 actually responded before attempting the jump.

That jump script exposed another failure mode. The first version tried to SSH into the Mac every time I connected to the VPS. It worked while the tunnel stayed up, but after the tunnel dropped it left me with a hanging shell and no feedback. The better version checked the port first, used a short connect timeout, and dropped me into a normal VPS shell as a fallback. Small change, but it turned an unreliable experience into one I could trust.

Then tmux caused another problem. A session created under one terminal environment did not always attach cleanly from another. In my case, xterm-ghostty on the Mac caused problems when the same session got reattached from a mobile client. Setting a more portable default terminal type fixed it and reminded me that session portability depends on the assumptions baked into it.

None of these looked dramatic. Together, these half-solved problems can turn a clever setup into one you stop using after a week.

And Then the Tooling Caught Up

Right around the time I had this working reliably, Anthropic shipped two features that cover a lot of the same ground.

Remote Control lets you continue a local Claude Code session from your phone or any browser. It runs on your machine (your filesystem, your tools, your project config) with the phone just acting as a window into that session. No port forwarding, no VPS, no reverse tunnel.

Dispatch goes further. You message a task from your phone, and it spawns a session on your Mac to handle it. You do not even need to have a session running already.

So did I waste my time? Honestly, I do not think so. Remote Control allows one connection per session and times out after about ten minutes of network loss, an awkward limit on spotty mobile data on a rural train line. My setup survives longer outages because mosh and autossh handle exactly that. And the VPS gives me a general-purpose foothold beyond Claude Code, including a shell when I need one.

If I started fresh today with a stable connection and needed only Claude Code access from my phone, I would try Remote Control first and probably never build any of this.

The Lesson Worth Keeping

I have run into the same trade-off with infrastructure, AI tooling, and the house we built last year. An initial design can look clean before details such as an unreliable connection or an existing work VPN force it to change. The result may look stranger, but each piece addresses a constraint.

Tools also catch up, and the constraints can change. The setup I built still helps me, but I would not recommend every part of it to someone starting today. Understanding why each piece existed made it easy to decide which ones I could drop once better options showed up.

I still use this setup on train rides, and I would start with Remote Control if I needed only Claude Code access.

item.title: Growing Wolt+ across signup and delivery pricing
item.description: I led client work for Wolt+ signup and long-distance delivery across iOS, Android, and web. The cart and checkout experiments contributed to about 30% growth in membership sign-ups.
item.content:encoded:
Context

I worked on several Wolt+ membership initiatives during 2024 and 2025. The work covered two related problems: making subscription signup easier during an order, and giving members useful delivery discounts outside the free-delivery radius.

As the client DRI across iOS, Android, and web, I worked with backend, product, design, QA, and data teams while implementing the iOS side myself. Because the changes appeared in discovery, venue, cart, and checkout screens, decisions about one surface often affected another.

Signup experiments

The first proposal combined a new cart entry point with an express signup flow. I pushed to run them as independent experiments. Shipping the cart entry point first meant we could learn whether the new placement changed sign-ups without waiting for the more complex signup work.

Express signup used a multi-step bottom sheet, a pattern the client did not support at the time. I also simplified the transition between express and full signup and coordinated payment and backend edge cases.

Some early A/B results gave a misleading picture. I worked with data science to review the instrumentation and understand what the experiment measured before using it to guide another release. The cart and checkout subscription work ultimately contributed to about 30% growth in membership sign-ups.

Long-distance delivery

Wolt+ offered free delivery within a defined radius. Long-distance delivery extended the membership benefit with discounted delivery pricing outside that radius. The clients had to keep the price and eligibility consistent in discovery lists, on the venue page, and at checkout.

I worked with the frontend and backend teams on the API structure and naming because the same concepts had to work across several screens and client implementations.

I also designed a reusable bottom sheet that explained the delivery price and Wolt+ savings across entry points.

Results

Both signup experiments went through testing and rollout, and the cart entry point remained a subscription surface. Long-distance delivery also rolled out across multiple app surfaces after positive A/B test results. Together, the projects made Wolt+ visible during the order flow and gave members outside the free radius a clearer benefit.

What I'd do next

The projects depended on several teams and analytics definitions. If I revisited the work, I would write the shared pricing terms and experiment events into the client RFC earlier, with examples for each surface. That would give design, backend, data science, and client engineers one place to review assumptions before implementation and analysis diverged.

item.title: Making iOS telemetry easier to inspect and debug
item.description: I built a macOS client that receives iOS telemetry over a local WebSocket, then added search and filtering so engineers could verify events without interrupting their work.
item.content:encoded:
Context

At Wolt, engineers could inspect analytics events in a full-screen view inside the iOS app. It worked, but using it during feature development took too long. The view had no search or filtering, and opening it took over the screen where I tested the feature. Finding one event in a busy session meant reading through everything around it. This made ordinary validation work harder for engineers and product teams: checking a new event, debugging unexpected data, and reviewing instrumentation before release. The viewer displayed the payloads but did not provide a quick way to narrow them to the event or field under investigation.

I initiated and built Telemetry Viewer independently to shorten that loop. I wanted an engineer to keep using the app normally while watching its events on a Mac.

What I built

The iOS app streams telemetry events over a local WebSocket to a macOS client. The desktop app shows the event names and payloads sent to backend systems, with search and filtering for narrowing a session to the data under investigation. The event view exposed the complete payload sent to backend systems, so the same client covered both event names and field-level checks.

Keeping the viewer on macOS left the phone available for the test flow.

Rollout

I first shared the tool with a small group of engineers, then demonstrated it more broadly and supported adoption by additional engineers. I developed it from the initial concept through adoption across teams.

I also worked with an Android engineer who built a similar tool for that client. The same approach supported privacy-related telemetry work where teams needed to inspect exactly which data the app emitted.

Results

Teams used Telemetry Viewer to verify analytics, debug unexpected events, and check instrumentation for experiments. Moving inspection off the phone made those checks faster and let engineers keep the feature under test visible. Teams also used it during release validation, which improved confidence that analytics changes matched the intended behavior before rollout.

What I'd do next

If I continued it, I would identify the searches and payload checks people repeat most often, then automate those workflows. I would also document a small compatibility contract for the iOS and Android implementations.

item.title: Test automation for weekly iOS regression testing
item.description: I maintained Maestro regression tests and built Python and agent-assisted tools for manual-test preparation, while checking accessibility, localization including right-to-left layouts, and telemetry as part of feature delivery.
item.content:encoded:
Context

My Wolt team ran weekly regression testing alongside feature development. We also held manual-testing sessions, which required test cases, Confluence pages, and Google Sheets for the team.

I worked on both sides of that process by maintaining UI tests and automating preparation for the manual sessions.

UI regression tests

I added and maintained Maestro UI tests for the team's weekly regression testing.

Manual-test preparation

I wrote Python scripts and agent-assisted workflows to prepare team manual-testing sessions. The workflow drafted test cases for review, then generated the Confluence pages and Google Sheets used to coordinate the session. It removed multiple hours of repetitive setup and coordination each time.

Feature validation

For features I owned, I checked accessibility and localization during implementation and regression testing, making sure each feature worked across the app's languages and locales, from Japanese to right-to-left Arabic and Hebrew.

Telemetry Viewer also contributed to release validation. The iOS app streamed analytics events over a local WebSocket to a macOS client with search and filtering. I used it to verify what a feature emitted, investigate unexpected events, and check experiment instrumentation without covering the phone with the old full-screen event viewer.

What I'd do next

If I returned to this work, I would document which regression checks belonged in Maestro, which required a manual session, and which needed telemetry verification. I would also measure setup time and recurring failures before choosing the next task to automate.

item.title: Replacing an article extraction pipeline safely
item.description: I built SmartView's second article extraction pipeline beside the existing implementation, with client-controlled rollout and fallback behavior for an app used by millions of people.
item.content:encoded:
Context

SmartView extracted and formatted publisher articles inside the SmartNews app. Millions of people used this core reading surface, and the existing pipeline had accumulated publisher-specific behavior over time. Replacing it in one switch would have made every parsing difference a release risk.

I led the iOS implementation of SmartView v2. The work had to improve the extraction code while preserving the existing renderer as a way back when a page or configuration did not behave as expected.

Parallel implementation

I built SmartHTMLExtractorV2 beside the first extractor instead of changing the old pipeline in place. The two implementations let us compare behavior and move traffic incrementally.

The new extractor lived in a Swift module named SmartHTML. I wrapped SwiftSoup behind an internal API rather than letting its types spread through the app. That boundary gave the extraction pipeline one place for HTML parsing and cleanup, and it kept a third-party parser from defining the rest of our rendering code.

The pipeline applied CSS rules delivered by backend services and converted the result into internal formatting models.

Rollout and fallback

Client conditions selected v1 or v2, so the two extractors could coexist during rollout. We could limit exposure while checking production content instead of moving all users to the new path at once.

I also added fallback behavior for failures in the client-condition configuration, including the stage and production URL choices used by the pipeline. Edition-aware proxy behavior kept the US and Japanese editions on their intended paths. Image selection accounted for iOS version as well, including JPEG and WebP support where appropriate.

Results

SmartView v2 shipped as a parallel rendering system with feature flags and fallback behavior. The team could validate the new extractor incrementally while the first implementation remained available. The rollout completed without regressions to the existing article-reading experience during the migration. The new Swift module also provided a smaller boundary for future parsing and formatting work inside a mixed Objective-C and Swift codebase.

What I'd do next

I would next define the evidence needed to retire v1, including representative publisher samples, edition coverage, configuration failures, and supported iOS versions. Once those checks passed, I would remove the old path and the branching that existed only for migration.

item.title: Building SmartNews's 2020 election coverage
item.description: I built iOS features for SmartNews's 2020 US election coverage, including perspective controls, candidate and results widgets, and edition-aware behavior under a fixed election-day deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Context

SmartNews's 2020 US election work had a deadline that could not move. Teams in Tokyo and San Francisco worked on several connected features for the US edition, including ways to compare political coverage, follow candidates, and see election results.

I worked on the iOS implementation across those surfaces. We needed the UI, API data, visibility windows, language rules, deep links, and telemetry ready before election day.

News From All Sides

For News From All Sides, I built a News Event view around a custom UISlider. The control supported either three or five positions depending on the available perspectives.

I also added onboarding, deep links, action logging, and entry points from multiple parts of the app. The feature dealt with politically sensitive material, so the control had to make the available perspectives clear without assigning meaning beyond the data.

Candidates and results

I implemented candidate widgets and lists, along with an election-results widget. Start and end timestamps controlled when the results surface appeared.

Language also depended on the SmartNews edition, not only the device locale. I added edition-aware rules so the Japanese edition displayed Japanese where required even when the system language differed.

The API integrations included fallback behavior, and client conditions controlled rollout.

Delivery

The election features shipped by election day across the intended app surfaces. Users could move among different political perspectives, browse candidate information, and see results when the configured time window opened. The implementation also recorded interactions so the teams could understand how people used the new entry points and controls.

What I'd do next

Time-based UI is easy to test in the middle of its valid window and easy to get wrong at the boundaries. For a future election release in the same product, I would add a shared clock abstraction and focused tests for the start time, end time, missing timestamps, and edition changes. I would run those cases against both editions and record the expected screen state beside each timestamp. The same test plan would cover an unavailable API response and a disabled client condition, so the team could see which rule controlled the screen without reconstructing the release logic near another fixed deadline. I would also document which fallback should win when API availability, client conditions, and the election schedule disagree.
